q.intro.text: A right triangle on grid paper: its legs are three inches and four inches, and each grid square is one inch. How long is the slanted side? Pick an answer and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s0.text: The square corner is the right angle. The side across from it is the hypotenuse, c. The two sides that make the right angle are the legs, a and b.

e.s1.text: A square on the three inch leg covers three times three, nine square inches. On the four inch leg: four times four, sixteen. That is what a squared and b squared mean: areas of squares.

e.s2.text: The square on c is tilted, so surround it: the upright square around it is seven by seven, forty-nine. Take away the four corner triangles of six each: c squared is forty-nine minus twenty-four, twenty-five.

e.s3.text: Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five: the two leg squares together cover the hypotenuse square exactly. So c is the square root of twenty-five: five inches.

e.rule.text: It works for every right triangle: a squared plus b squared equals c squared. This is the Pythagorean theorem.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is the slanted side five inches, and not seven?

e.why-ok.text: Yes. The side of a square is the number that, times itself, makes its area: five times five is twenty-five.

e.why-add.text: Walking along both legs is three plus four, seven inches. The slanted side cuts across the corner, so it is shorter: five inches.

e.why-area.text: Twenty-five is the area of the square, in square inches. The side is the number that times itself makes twenty-five: five.

t.intro.text: Your turn: legs of six inches and eight inches. The first two steps are done for you.

t.area.text: What is the area of the square on the hypotenuse, c squared?

t.area-ok.text: Yes: thirty-six plus sixty-four is one hundred square inches. The two leg squares fill the hypotenuse square.

t.area-add.text: Fourteen adds the side lengths, six plus eight. The theorem adds the areas of the squares: thirty-six plus sixty-four.

t.area-sub.text: The square on the hypotenuse is the biggest one: the two leg squares together cover it. Thirty-six plus sixty-four is what?

t.area-side.text: Ten inches is a side. The question asks for the area of the square on the hypotenuse.

t.area-no.text: The two leg squares together cover the hypotenuse square. Add their areas.

t.c.text: Now the side: how long is the hypotenuse, c?

t.c-ok.text: Yes: ten times ten is one hundred, so c is the square root of one hundred, ten inches.

t.c-area.text: One hundred is the area of the square. The side is the number that times itself makes one hundred.

t.c-half.text: Fifty is half of one hundred. A square root is not half: which number times itself makes one hundred?

t.c-add.text: Six plus eight walks along both legs. The hypotenuse cuts across the corner, so it is shorter.

t.c-no.text: Which number times itself makes one hundred?

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked five inches, and you were right. Now you can show why: the two leg squares add up to the hypotenuse square.

t.cb-add.text: At the start you picked seven inches. That adds the legs, but the slanted side cuts across the corner. Add the squares, not the sides.

t.cb-count.text: At the start you picked six inches, maybe by counting the grid squares the slanted side crosses. Most of them it only clips. The areas tell the truth: five inches.

t.cb-none.text: Square the legs, add, take the square root. That is how every hypotenuse is found.

p.intro.text: Sam checked two right triangles, three four five and six eight ten: both work. Sam says: so a squared plus b squared equals c squared is true for every right triangle. Is Sam’s check a proof?

p.yes.text: Two examples can’t cover every right triangle. Here is an argument that can. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build.text: Right: examples are not a proof. Here is an argument that is. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Four equal sides and four right angles: the middle is a square, c by c.

p.c2.text: Right. The triangles slide into two rectangles, a by b. Uncovered: a square on a and a square on b.

p.c3.text: Right. Same big square, same four triangles, so the same area is uncovered: c squared equals a squared plus b squared.

p.no-looks.text: Looks can fool you. The reason is the angles: the two sharp angles of a right triangle add to ninety degrees, so each corner is one hundred eighty minus ninety, ninety degrees.

p.no-ex.text: Examples are what Sam had. This argument never uses particular numbers, so it works for any right triangle.

p.no-area.text: a squared and b squared are areas of squares on the legs, not the area of the triangle.

p.no-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: it never used particular numbers, so it holds for every right triangle. And it needs the right angle: the ninety degree corners made the middle a square.
